title: Locality-Aware Tiling and Expert Coalescing: Long-Context MoE Performance Notes
content:
Summary:

Quick notes from experiments in Feb 2025 exploring an orthogonal approach to the usual routing+prefetch story: instead of only optimizing routing fanout and prefetch timing, try to reduce cross-expert memory movement by (A) tiling KV and attention kernels to increase token locality and (B) coalescing small expert dispatches into a fused 'micro-batched' expert kernel when experts are hot but individually low-util.

Why this felt promising:
- On long-context (64k+) workloads with MoE backbones, we see two dominant overheads besides compute: many tiny scatter/gather operations for expert activations, and repeated KV cache reads/writes that defeat L2/L1 locality.
- Typical mitigation (larger batches, aggressive prefetch) helps throughput but hurts tail latency and increases working memory. If we can change the shape of memory traffic we can reduce memcpy and PCIe/NVLink churn for private/dedicated deployments.

What we attempted (high level):
1) Locality-aware tiling: tile KV read/writes and attention matmul by grouping contiguous token ranges across the fused sequence rather than per-request token ranges. The idea: when multiple requests share prefix tokens (or when a single long-context request spans many tiles), ensure we read contiguous KV pages and keep them resident across multiple layers.

2) Expert coalescing (micro-batching at kernel level): when the router selects many experts with small per-expert batch size (e.g., 1-8 tokens), instead of launching a per-expert kernel we collect tokens destined to the same physical GPU and run a fused expert kernel with a custom index mapping. This reduces kernel launch overhead, reduces frequent device-to-device memcpy (NVLink) for expert gather/scatter, and enables better thread/block occupancy.

3) Hybrid scheduling: combine 1+2 and add a light-weight heuristic in the scheduler that decides when to coalesce vs. dispatch normally based on expected p99 impact and memory headroom. Heuristic uses: expected expert fanout, per-expert token count, current GPU SM occupancy, and KV working set size.

Experiment setup:
- Models: LLaMA-2-13B MoE (custom MoE head), Mistral-XL with MoE patch, Qwen-MoE (experimental).
- HW: A100-80GB (single-node), H100-80GB (single-node), Dual-A100 NVLink (for cross-GPU expert offload tests).
- Workloads: synthetic long-context continuations (64k, 128k), customer chat logs replay (variable prefix sharing), and stressfanout (many short requests mapped to many experts).
- Baseline: current runtime (no coalescing, existing prefetch policy), and a variant with aggressive prefetching but no tiling/coalescing.

Key metrics captured:
- end-to-end p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) per request
- per-token GPU SM utilization and achieved TFLOPS
- device-to-device memcpy counts and total bytes (nvprof/CUPTI counters)
- kernel launch count per request and average kernel duration
- memory stall counters (L2/DRAM BW, L1 hit/miss where available)

Observed results (high level):
- Coalescing reduced kernel launch count by ~40-70% for high-fanout small-token cases, with p50 token throughput improving 20-35% on A100 and H100.
- p99 improved most when prefix sharing was high (multiple requests sharing large prefixes); in that scenario locality-aware tiling kept KV pages resident and reduced DRAM reads by ~28% measured via CUPTI DRAM counters.
- For purely random per-request tokens (no prefix sharing), coalescing sometimes increased tail-latency due to added scheduling jitter; hybrid heuristic prevented most regressions by falling back to normal dispatch when per-expert token count > 32.
- Device-to-device traffic for expert activations dropped substantially (30-60%) when coalescing fused cross-GPU movements into larger, fewer transfers (better NVLink utilization).

Profiling takeaways (practical):
- Kernel launch overhead matters more than expected in MoE when per-expert workload is small. Measure kernel_count/request in traces (we added a per-request counter in the runtime tracing).
- NVTX ranges + per-kernel timers are essential; but also log cups of memcpy sizes — the distribution is more informative than totals. Many tiny memcpys indicate a scheduling/shape problem.
- On H100 the benefit curve shifts — fused kernels see larger relative gains due to better async copies and SAMPA scheduling, but also require careful shared memory tuning to avoid bank conflicts.

Micro-implementation notes (what we changed in code):
- Added a CoalescePlanner component that receives a list of expert dispatch intents (expert_id, token_idx, layer) and outputs groups with mapping tables. The groups are constrained by per-group token budget and total scratch memory.
- Implemented fused_expert_kernel_{a100,h100}.cu which consumes mapping tables and an offsets buffer. The kernel writes outputs back into the global scatter buffer using the mapping.
- Tiling changed for KV read: .kv_tile_size parameter (default 256 tokens) that slides with overlap 0 for now. We keep a small LRU for active tiles per GPU to avoid reloading when nearby layers access the same KV ranges.
- Added telemetry: per-request kernel_count, memcpy_ops, coalesced_groups_created, tiles_resident_peak. Recorded as structured tags in traces.

Open problems / surprises:
- Memory fragmentation: coalescing can increase transient scratch allocations which interact poorly with our allocator on heavy burst loads. We mitigated with a pool of pre-allocated mapping buffers but still see fragmentation on corner cases.
- Mapping table overhead: for very large groupings the mapping table itself becomes a non-trivial memcpy cost. We observed diminishing returns past ~2048 tokens coalesced per group.
- Prefetch interplay: aggressive prefetch into coalesced groups can increase DRAM pressure; we need a joint policy that considers tiles_resident_peak when prefetching.
- Some Qwen-MoE variants have very different expert parameter layouts; fused kernels needed small shape-specializations to avoid 20% slowdown from unaligned memory access.

Action items / next steps:
- Short (1–2 weeks): increase telemetry collection to include mapping table memcpy bytes, and add a conservative coalescing threshold tuned per-GPU (A100 vs H100). Create a follow-up perf PR to gate coalescing behind a runtime flag.
- Medium (3–6 weeks): run full fleet shadow tests on Dedicated pools with representative customer workloads (chat+backfill) to observe real-world p99 changes. Tune hybrid heuristic using historical traces for expected fanout distributions.
- Long: explore compiler-assisted fused kernels generated per-model at rollout time (auto-tune mapping table packing and shared memory layout). This could open up more gains without manual specialization per model.

Back-of-envelope economics thought: if coalescing reduces average token GPU-time by 15% and reduces cross-GPU traffic substantially, Dedicated customers could see unit-cost reductions; but need to quantify memory overhead tradeoffs to avoid increased host-side latency.

Quick checklist for reviewers / PR notes:
- Does the scheduler heuristic sound safe for production? (it is conservative: avoids coalescing if expected per-expert tokens > 32 or if tiles_resident_peak > 70% memcap)
- Are the fused kernel interfaces acceptable for adding per-model specializations? (we exposed a small vtable and a codegen hook to insert shape-specialized kernels)
- Please review telemetry names: "coalesced_groups_created", "mapping_table_bytes", "tiles_resident_peak" — want these consistent with console dashboards.

Notes to self:
- Benchmark scripts used: scripts/long_context/tiling_coalesce_runner.py (local only, not checked in yet).
- Relevant tickets: JIRA-RT-4472 (coalescing design), JIRA-RT-4490 (alloc fragmentation), GH PR 2183 (initial fused kernel).
- Chat thread: #eng-serving-runtime on slack has early perf traces, timestamped Feb 18 for H100 runs.

Unresolved design question to discuss in sync: should coalescing be model-aware (different thresholds per architecture) or purely workload-aware? My leaning: hybrid: default workload heuristic then optional model-specific overrides pushed during model onboarding if customers request.

End.

-- Ethan
